title: Hávamál
translation: Henry Adams Bellows, The Poetic Edda (1923)
note: The verses are from Henry Adams Bellows' English translation of the Poetic Edda (1923), which is in the public domain. Stanza numbers follow that translation. The 'means' lines are written for children. All stanzas; set for reading aloud (words unchanged).

verses.verse:
Within the gates ere a man shall go,
Full warily let him watch,
Full long let him look about him.
For little he knows where a foe may lurk,
And sit in the seats within
verses.means:
When you go into a new place, stop and take a good look around first.
It is wise to know who is there before you walk in.

verses.verse:
Hail to the giver! a guest has come.
Where shall the stranger sit??
Swift shall he be who, with swords shall try,
The proof of his might to make
verses.means:
A guest has come, so thank the host and find the newcomer a seat quickly.
Do not leave a stranger waiting, unsure of their place.

verses.verse:
Fire he needs who with frozen knees,
Has come from the cold without.
Food and clothes must the farer have,
The man from the mountains come
verses.means:
Someone who comes in from the cold needs a warm fire, food and dry clothes.
When a traveler comes to your home, help them get warm and fed.

verses.verse:
Water and towels and welcoming speech,
Should he find who comes, to the feast.
If renown he would get, and again be greeted,
Wisely and well must he act
verses.means:
A guest should be given water, a towel and kind words of welcome.
And a guest who wants to be welcomed again should behave well and wisely.

verses.verse:
Wits must he have who wanders wide,
But all is easy at home.
At the witless man the wise shall wink,
When among such men he sits
verses.means:
When you travel far from home, you need your wits about you, because things are easier at home.
Wise people notice when someone acts without thinking.

verses.verse:
A man shall not boast of his keenness of mind,
But keep it close in his breast.
To the silent and wise does ill come seldom,
When he goes as guest to a house.
For a faster friend one never finds,
Than wisdom tried and true
verses.means:
Don't brag about how clever you are.
Quiet, wise guests rarely get into trouble, and good sense is the best friend you can have.

verses.verse:
The knowing guest who goes to the feast,
In silent attention sits.
With his ears he hears, with his eyes he watches,
Thus wary are wise men all
verses.means:
A wise guest sits quietly, listens with their ears and watches with their eyes.
Paying attention is how wise people learn.

verses.verse:
Happy the one who wins for himself,
Favor and praises fair.
Less safe by far is the wisdom found,
That is hid in another's heart
verses.means:
It is a happy thing to earn kind words by what you do.
Your own good sense is safer to trust than ideas hidden in someone else's heart.

verses.verse:
Happy the man who has while he lives,
Wisdom and praise as well,
For evil counsel a man full oft,
Has from another's heart
verses.means:
Be glad if you have both wisdom and a good name.
Bad advice often comes from other people, so learn to think for yourself.

verses.verse:
A better burden may no man bear,
For wanderings wide than wisdom.
It is better than wealth on unknown ways,
And in grief a refuge it gives
verses.means:
Wisdom is the best thing to carry on a long trip.
It is worth more than money in a strange place, and it helps you when you are sad.

verses.verse:
A better burden may no man bear,
For wanderings wide than wisdom.
Worse food for the journey he brings not afield,
Than an over-drinking of ale
verses.means:
Wisdom is the best thing to carry on a journey.
Drinking too much is the worst.

verses.verse:
Less good there lies than most believe,
In ale for mortal men.
For the more he drinks the less does man,
Of his mind the mastery hold
verses.means:
Ale is not as good for people as many think.
The more someone drinks, the less they control their own mind.

verses.verse:
Over beer the bird of forgetfulness broods,
And steals the minds of men.
With the heron's feathers fettered I lay,
And in Gunnloth's house was held
verses.means:
The High One teaches from his own journey.
Forgetfulness hovers over the ale cup, and he tells of the night in Gunnloth's hall when it held even him.

verses.verse:
Drunk I was, I was dead-drunk,
When with Fjalar wise I was.
'Tis the best of drinking if back one brings,
His wisdom with him home
verses.means:
The High One shares a lesson he learned himself.
The best drinking is the kind where you bring your wisdom home with you.

verses.verse:
The son of a king shall be silent and wise,
And bold in battle as well.
Bravely and gladly a man shall go,
Till the day of his death is come
verses.means:
A king's son should be quiet, wise and brave.
Everyone should go through life with courage and a glad heart, all their days.

verses.verse:
The sluggard believes he shall live forever,
If the fight he faces not.
But age shall not grant him the gift of peace,
Though spears may spare his life
verses.means:
A lazy person thinks that running from hard things will keep them safe forever.
But nobody can run away from growing older, so it is better to be brave.

verses.verse:
The fool is agape when he comes to the feast,
He stammers or else is still.
But soon if he gets a drink is it seen,
What the mind of the man is like
verses.means:
A foolish guest stares and stammers.
Give them a drink, and their true nature soon shows.

verses.verse:
He alone is aware who has wandered wide,
And far abroad has fared,
How great a mind is guided by him,
That wealth of wisdom has
verses.means:
People who have traveled far and seen a lot can tell how wise someone else is.
Seeing the world helps you understand people.

verses.verse:
Shun not the mead, but drink in measure.
Speak to the point or be still.
For rudeness none shall rightly blame thee,
If soon thy bed thou seekest
verses.means:
Enjoy good things, but don't have too much.
Say what you mean or stay quiet, and nobody will call you rude for going to bed in good time.

verses.verse:
The greedy man, if his mind be vague,
Will eat till sick he is.
The vulgar man, when among the wise,
To scorn by his belly is brought
verses.means:
A greedy person eats until they feel sick.
Eating too much can make others laugh at you, so eat what you need and stop there.

verses.verse:
The herds know well when home they shall fare,
And then from the grass they go.
But the foolish man his belly's measure,
Shall never know aright
verses.means:
Even cows know when they have eaten enough and it is time to go home.
A foolish person never learns how much is enough.

verses.verse:
A paltry man and poor of mind,
At all things ever mocks.
For never he knows, what he ought to know,
That he is not free from faults
verses.means:
Someone with a small mind makes fun of everything.
What they never learn is that they have faults too.

verses.verse:
The witless man is awake all night,
Thinking of many things.
Care-worn he is when the morning comes,
And his woe is just as it was
verses.means:
Someone who doesn't think clearly lies awake all night worrying.
In the morning they are tired, and the problem is still the same.

verses.verse:
The foolish man for friends all those,
Who laugh at him will hold.
When among the wise he marks it not,
Though hatred of him they speak
verses.means:
A foolish person thinks everyone who laughs at them is a friend.
They don't even notice when people are being unkind to them.

verses.verse:
The foolish man for friends all those,
Who laugh at him will hold.
But the truth when he comes to the council he learns,
That few in his favor will speak
verses.means:
A foolish person thinks everyone who laughs at them is a friend.
But when they need help, they find out that few will speak up for them.

verses.verse:
An ignorant man thinks that all he knows,
When he sits by himself in a corner.
But never what answer to make he knows,
When others with questions come
verses.means:
Someone who sits alone may think they know everything.
But when others ask them questions, they have no answers.

verses.verse:
A witless man, when he meets with men,
Had best in silence abide.
For no one shall find that nothing he knows,
If his mouth is not open too much.
But a man knows not, if nothing he knows,
When his mouth has been open too much
verses.means:
If you don't know much about something, it is often best to stay quiet and listen.
Nobody will notice what you don't know unless you talk too much.

verses.verse:
Wise shall he seem who well can question,
And also answer well.
Nought is concealed that men may say,
Among the sons of men
verses.means:
Wise people know how to ask good questions and give good answers.
Whatever people say gets passed around, so choose your words with care.

verses.verse:
Often he speaks who never is still,
With words that win no faith.
The babbling tongue, if a bridle it find not,
Oft for itself sings ill
verses.means:
Someone who never stops talking says lots of things nobody believes.
A tongue that never rests often gets its owner into trouble.

verses.verse:
In mockery no one a man shall hold,
Although he fare to the feast.
Wise seems one oft, if nought he is asked,
And safely he sits dry-skinned
verses.means:
Don't make fun of anyone, even at a party.
A guest who sits quietly and isn't put on the spot stays safe and comfortable.

verses.verse:
Wise a guest holds it to take to his heels,
When mock of another he makes.
But little he knows who laughs at the feast,
Though he mocks in the midst of his foes
verses.means:
A guest who makes fun of someone may soon need to run!
Laughing at people can turn them against you, even when you don't notice it.

verses.verse:
Friendly of mind are many men,
Till feasting they mock at their friends.
To mankind a bane must it ever be,
When guests together strive
verses.means:
Lots of people are friendly until they start teasing their friends at a party.
When guests quarrel, it is bad for everyone.

verses.verse:
Oft should one make an early meal,
Nor fasting come to the feast.
Else he sits and chews as if he would choke,
And little is able to ask
verses.means:
Have a little something to eat before a big meal.
If you arrive very hungry, you will be too busy chewing to talk with anyone.

verses.verse:
Crooked and far is the road to a foe,
Though his house on the highway be.
But wide and straight is the way to a friend,
Though far away he fare
verses.means:
The road to someone who doesn't like you feels long and crooked, even if they live close by.
The road to a friend feels wide and straight, even if they live far away.

verses.verse:
Forth shall one go, nor stay as a guest,
In a single spot forever.
Love becomes loathing if long one sits,
By the hearth in another's home
verses.means:
A good guest knows when it is time to go home.
Even the warmest welcome wears thin if you stay too long.

verses.verse:
Better a house, though a hut it be,
A man is master at home.
A pair of goats and a patched-up roof,
Are better far than begging
verses.means:
A little home of your own is better than none, because at home you are in charge.
Two goats and a patched roof are far better than having to beg.

verses.verse:
Better a house, though a hut it be,
A man is master at home.
His heart is bleeding who needs must beg,
When food he fain would have
verses.means:
A little home of your own is a good thing to have.
It hurts the heart to have to ask others for every meal.

verses.verse:
Away from his arms in the open field,
A man should fare not a foot.
For never he knows when the need for a spear,
Shall arise on the distant road
verses.means:
In the old days, a traveler kept their weapons close.
You never knew what danger waited on the road.
Be prepared when you set out.

verses.verse:
If wealth a man has won for himself,
Let him never suffer in need.
Oft he saves for a foe what he plans for a friend,
For much goes worse than we wish
verses.means:
If you have worked hard for what you have, don't go without the things you need.
Things don't always turn out the way we plan.

verses.verse:
None so free with gifts or food have I found,
That gladly he took not a gift,
Nor one who so widely scattered his wealth,
That of recompense hatred he had
verses.means:
Even the most generous person is glad to get a gift.
And nobody who gives a lot minds being given something back.

verses.verse:
Friends shall gladden each other with arms and garments,
As each for himself can see.
Gift-givers' friendships are longest found,
If fair their fates may be
verses.means:
Friends make each other happy by giving each other useful things.
Friends who give to each other stay friends the longest.

verses.verse:
To his friend a man a friend shall prove,
And gifts with gifts requite.
But men shall mocking with mockery answer,
And fraud with falsehood meet
verses.means:
Be a true friend to your friends, and return their gifts with gifts.
People who mock and deceive will be met the same way.

verses.verse:
To his friend a man a friend shall prove,
To him and the friend of his friend.
But never a man shall friendship make,
With one of his foeman's friends
verses.means:
Be a true friend to your friend, and to your friend's friends too.
Stay loyal to the people who stand by you.

verses.verse:
If a friend thou hast whom thou fully wilt trust,
And good from him wouldst get,
Thy thoughts with his mingle, and gifts shalt thou make,
And fare to find him oft
verses.means: When you have a friend you trust, share your thoughts with them, give them gifts and go to see them often.

verses.verse:
If another thou hast whom thou hardly wilt trust,
Yet good from him wouldst get,
Thou shalt speak him fair, but falsely think,
And fraud with falsehood requite
verses.means: With someone you cannot trust, be polite, but keep your real thoughts to yourself.

verses.verse:
So is it with him whom thou hardly wilt trust,
And whose mind thou mayst not know.
Laugh with him mayst thou, but speak not thy mind,
Like gifts to his shalt thou give
verses.means: With someone whose mind you cannot read, you can laugh together, but do not share your secrets.

verses.verse:
Young was I once, and wandered alone,
And nought of the road I knew.
Rich did I feel when a comrade I found,
For man is man's delight
verses.means:
Once I was young and traveled alone, and I didn't know the way.
I felt rich when I found a friend, because people bring each other joy.

verses.verse:
The lives of the brave and noble are best,
Sorrows they seldom feed.
But the coward fear of all things feels,
And not gladly the niggard gives
verses.means:
Brave, good-hearted people live the best lives and don't dwell on sorrow.
Someone who is afraid of everything is never at ease, and a stingy person never likes to give.

verses.verse:
My garments once in a field I gave,
To a pair of carven poles.
Heroes they seemed when clothes they had,
But the naked man is nought
verses.means:
Once I put my clothes on two carved wooden posts in a field, and they looked like heroes!
How you dress and look after yourself changes how others see you.

verses.verse:
On the hillside drear the fir-tree dies,
All bootless its needles and bark.
It is like a man whom no one loves,
Why should his life be long?
verses.means:
A tree alone on a bare hillside withers away.
A person whom no one loves is the same.
We all need each other.

verses.verse:
Hotter than fire between false friends,
Does friendship five days burn.
When the sixth day comes the fire cools,
And ended is all the love
verses.means:
Friendship between people who aren't truly friends can burn hotter than fire for five days.
On the sixth day the fire goes out, and that friendship is over.

verses.verse:
No great thing needs a man to give,
Oft little will purchase praise.
With half a loaf and a half-filled cup,
A friend full fast I made
verses.means:
You don't need to give big presents to make a friend.
Sharing half a loaf of bread and a cup can be enough.

verses.verse:
A little sand has a little sea,
And small are the minds of men.
Though all men are not equal in wisdom,
Yet half-wise only are all
verses.means:
A small beach has only a little sea.
Some people are wiser than others, but nobody knows everything.

verses.verse:
A measure of wisdom each man shall have,
But never too much let him know.
The fairest lives do those men live,
Whose wisdom wide has grown
verses.means:
Everyone should have a good amount of wisdom, but nobody needs to know everything.
The happiest lives belong to people who know a good many things.

verses.verse:
A measure of wisdom each man shall have,
But never too much let him know.
For the wise man's heart is seldom happy,
If wisdom too great he has won
verses.means:
Be wise enough, but don't try to know everything.
A heart that carries too much knowing is not often happy.

verses.verse:
A measure of wisdom each man shall have,
But never too much let him know.
Let no man the fate before him see,
For so is he freest from sorrow
verses.means:
Be wise enough, but you don't need to know everything.
Not knowing what tomorrow brings lets you live without worrying about it.

verses.verse:
A brand from a brand is kindled and burned,
And fire from fire begotten.
And man by his speech is known to men,
And the stupid by their stillness
verses.means:
One flame lights another flame.
In the same way, people get to know you by the way you talk with them.

verses.verse:
He must early go forth who fain the blood,
Or the goods of another would get.
The wolf that lies idle shall win little meat,
Or the sleeping man success
verses.means:
The one who wants something must get up early.
A sleeping wolf catches nothing, and a sleeping person wins nothing.

verses.verse:
He must early go forth whose workers are few,
Himself his work to seek.
Much remains undone for the morning-sleeper,
For the swift is wealth half won
verses.means:
If you have a lot to do and not many helpers, get started early.
A late sleeper leaves things undone, and starting quickly gets the job half done.

verses.verse:
Of seasoned shingles and strips of bark,
For the thatch let one know his need,
And how much of wood he must have for a month,
Or in half a year he will use
verses.means:
Know how much wood and bark you will need for your roof and your fire.
It is wise to plan ahead for the months to come.

verses.verse:
Washed and fed to the council fare,
But care not too much for thy clothes.
Let none be ashamed of his shoes and hose,
Less still of the steed he rides,
Though poor be the horse he has
verses.means:
Go to important places clean and with a full tummy, but don't worry too much about your clothes.
Nobody should feel ashamed of their shoes, or of a horse that isn't fancy.

verses.verse:
When the eagle comes to the ancient sea,
He snaps and hangs his head.
So is a man in the midst of a throng,
Who few to speak for him finds
verses.means:
When an eagle reaches the sea, it hangs its head.
A person feels the same way in a crowd when nobody there will speak up for them.

verses.verse:
To question and answer must all be ready,
Who wish to be known as wise.
Tell one thy thoughts, but beware of two,
All know what is known to three
verses.means:
A wise person is ready to ask and to answer.
Tell one person your secret, but not two.
What three people know, everyone knows.

verses.verse:
The man who is prudent a measured use,
Of the might he has will make.
He finds when among the brave he fares,
That the boldest he may not be
verses.means:
A sensible person uses their strength with care.
When they are among brave people, they find out they may not be the boldest one there.

verses.verse:
Oft for the words that to others one speaks,
He will get but an evil gift
verses.means:
Part of this stanza is lost.
What remains says that careless words to others can come back to us as trouble.

verses.verse:
Too early to many a meeting I came,
And some too late have I sought.
The beer was all drunk, or not yet brewed.
Little the loathed man finds
verses.means:
Sometimes we arrive too early, and sometimes too late.
Timing matters, and the unwelcome guest finds little.

verses.verse:
To their homes men would bid me hither and yon,
If at meal-time I needed no meat,
Or would hang two hams in my true friend's house,
Where only one I had eaten
verses.means:
People would gladly invite me, if I did not need feeding.
Be honest about whose generosity is real.

verses.verse:
Fire for men is the fairest gift,
And power to see the sun.
Health as well, if a man may have it,
And a life not stained with sin
verses.means:
Fire and seeing the sun are the finest gifts.
Good health is a gift too, and so is a life lived without doing wrong.

verses.verse:
All wretched is no man, though never so sick.
Some from their sons have joy,
Some win it from kinsmen, and some from their wealth,
And some from worthy works
verses.means:
Nobody is completely unhappy, even when they are sick.
Some find joy in their children, some in their family, some in what they have, and some in good work.

verses.verse:
It is better to live than to lie a corpse,
The live man catches the cow.
I saw flames rise for the rich man's pyre,
And before his door he lay dead
verses.means:
Being alive is better than anything.
A living person can still work and hope.
The dead can do nothing more.

verses.verse:
The lame rides a horse, the handless is herdsman,
The deaf in battle is bold.
The blind man is better than one that is burned,
No good can come of a corpse
verses.means:
Everyone can still do something good.
Someone who cannot walk can ride.
Someone who cannot hear can be brave.
Life always has value.

verses.verse:
A son is better, though late he be born,
And his father to death have fared.
Memory-stones seldom stand by the road,
Save when kinsman honors his kin
verses.means:
A son is a blessing, even one born after his father has died.
Stones to remember people stand by the road because family members honor those who came before.

verses.verse:
Two make a battle, the tongue slays the head.
In each furry coat a fist I look for
verses.means:
It takes two to make a fight, and careless words can cost a life.
Be careful with your tongue.

verses.verse:
He welcomes the night whose fare is enough,
Short are the yards of a ship,
Uneasy are autumn nights.
Full oft does the weather change in a week,
And more in a month's time
verses.means:
Someone who has enough food is glad when night comes.
Autumn nights can be uneasy, and the weather can change a lot in a week, so it is good to be ready.

verses.verse:
A man knows not, if nothing he knows,
That gold oft apes begets.
One man is wealthy and one is poor,
Yet scorn for him none should know
verses.means:
Gold can make people act silly.
Some people are rich and some are poor, but nobody should be looked down on for being poor.

verses.verse:
Among Fitjung's sons saw I well-stocked folds,
Now bear they the beggar's staff.
Wealth is as swift as a winking eye,
Of friends the falsest it is
verses.means:
A family that was rich became poor.
Wealth can vanish in the blink of an eye.
It is the least faithful of friends.

verses.verse:
Cattle die, and kinsmen die,
And so one dies one's self.
But a noble name will never die,
If good renown one gets
verses.means:
Animals die, family members die, and one day each of us will too.
But a good name, earned by how you live, never dies.

verses.verse:
Cattle die, and kinsmen die,
And so one dies one's self.
One thing now that never dies,
The fame of a dead man's deeds
verses.means:
Everything that lives will one day die.
But the good things a person did are remembered long after they are gone.

verses.verse:
Certain is that which is sought from runes,
That the gods so great have made,
And the Master-Poet painted.
of the race of gods,
Silence is safest and best
verses.means:
Part of this stanza is lost.
It speaks of the runes the gods made, and ends with this: silence is safest and best.

verses.verse:
An unwise man, if a maiden's love,
Or wealth he chances to win,
His pride will wax, but his wisdom never,
Straight forward he fares in conceit
verses.means: When a foolish person wins love or wealth, their pride grows, but their wisdom does not.

verses.verse:
Give praise to the day at evening, to a woman on her pyre,
To a weapon which is tried, to a maid at wed lock,
To ice when it is crossed, to ale that is drunk
verses.means:
Do not praise something until it has proven itself.
Praise the day when evening comes, and ice once you have crossed it.

verses.verse:
When the gale blows hew wood, in fair winds seek the water.
Sport with maidens at dusk, for day's eyes are many.
From the ship seek swiftness, from the shield protection,
Cuts from the sword, from the maiden kisses
verses.means:
Do each thing at its right time.
Cut wood when the wind blows, and sail when the winds are fair.

verses.verse:
By the fire drink ale, over ice go on skates.
Buy a steed that is lean, and a sword when tarnished,
The horse at home fatten, the hound in thy dwelling
verses.means:
Use things in the way they work best.
Skate over ice, and choose a horse or sword for its true worth, not its looks.

verses.verse:
A man shall trust not the oath of a maid,
Nor the word a woman speaks.
For their hearts on a whirling wheel were fashioned,
And fickle their breasts were formed
verses.means: This stanza warns against trusting a promise too quickly, especially words spoken in love.

verses.verse:
In a breaking bow or a burning flame,
A ravening wolf or a croaking raven,
In a grunting boar, a tree with roots broken,
In billowy seas or a bubbling kettle
verses.means: Some things should never be trusted, like a breaking bow, a hungry wolf, or a boiling kettle.

verses.verse:
In a flying arrow or falling waters,
In ice new formed or the serpent's folds,
In a bride's bed-speech or a broken sword,
In the sport of bears or in sons of kings
verses.means: More things that cannot be trusted: a flying arrow, thin new ice, a broken sword.

verses.verse:
In a calf that is sick or a stubborn thrall,
A flattering witch or a foe new slain
verses.means: And still more things that cannot be trusted, like a sick calf or a flatterer.

verses.verse:
In a brother's slayer, if thou meet him abroad,
In a half-burned house, in a horse full swift,
One leg is hurt and the horse is useless,
None had ever such faith as to trust in them all
verses.means:
Do not put your trust in things that can turn on you.
No one should trust all of these.

verses.verse:
Hope not too surely for early harvest,
Nor trust too soon in thy son.
The field needs good weather, the son needs wisdom,
And oft is either denied
verses.means:
Do not count on things too early.
A field needs good weather, and a child needs time to grow wise.

verses.verse:
The love of women fickle of will,
Is like starting o'er ice with a steed unshod,
A two-year-old restive and little tamed,
Or steering a rudderless ship in a storm,
Or, lame, hunting reindeer on slippery rocks
verses.means: Love that changes its mind is as risky as riding a wild horse on ice, or steering a ship with no rudder in a storm.

verses.verse:
Clear now will I speak, for I know them both,
Men false to women are found.
When fairest we speak, then falsest we think,
Against wisdom we work with deceit
verses.means:
The High One speaks plainly, for he knows the hearts of both men and women.
Fair words can hide other thoughts, so he teaches us to look deeper.

verses.verse:
Soft words shall he speak and wealth shall he offer,
Who longs for a maiden's love,
And the beauty praise of the maiden bright.
He wins whose wooing is best
verses.means: Someone who hopes to win love speaks kindly and generously, and praises the one they love.

verses.verse:
Fault for loving let no man find,
Ever with any other.
Oft the wise are fettered, where fools go free,
By beauty that breeds desire
verses.means:
Do not blame anyone for falling in love.
Even wise people can be swept away by it.

verses.verse:
Fault with another let no man find,
For what touches many a man.
Wise men oft into witless fools,
Are made by mighty love
verses.means:
Do not blame others for what happens to so many people.
Love can make the wise act foolishly.

verses.verse:
The head alone knows what dwells near the heart,
A man knows his mind alone.
No sickness is worse to one who is wise,
Than to lack the longed-for joy
verses.means:
Only you truly know your own heart.
Nothing hurts more than longing for a joy you cannot have.

verses.verse:
This found I myself, when I sat in the reeds,
And long my love awaited.
As my life the maiden wise I loved,
Yet her I never had
verses.means:
The High One shares his own longing, for a wise maiden he loved and never won.
Even the wisest know the ache of a wish not granted.

verses.verse:
Billing's daughter I found on her bed,
In slumber bright as the sun.
Empty appeared an earl's estate,
Without that form so fair
verses.means: The High One begins the tale of Billing's daughter, whose beauty outshone a whole estate.

verses.verse:
"Othin, again at evening come,
If a woman thou wouldst win.
Evil it were if others than we,
Should know of such a sin."
verses.means: In the tale, the maiden tells the High One to come back at evening, and keep it secret.

verses.verse:
Away I hastened, hoping for joy,
And careless of counsel wise.
Well I believed that soon I should win,
Measureless joy with the maid
verses.means: Full of hope, the High One hurried on, trusting his heart over caution.

verses.verse:
So came I next when night it was,
The warriors all were awake.
With burning lights and waving brands,
I learned my luckess way
verses.means:
When he returned at night, the warriors were all awake, with torches burning and brands waving.
The way was barred.

verses.verse:
At morning then, when once more I came,
And all were sleeping still,
A dog found in the fair one's place,
Bound there upon her bed
verses.means:
At morning, he found only a dog bound in her place.
The maiden had matched his cleverness with her own.

verses.verse:
Many fair maids, if a man but tries them,
False to a lover are found.
That did I learn when I longed to gain,
With wiles the maiden wise.
Foul scorn was my meed from the crafty maid,
And nought from the woman I won
verses.means:
From this tale the High One draws a lesson for us.
Many a heart cannot be won by cunning, and he shares what he learned so we may be wiser.

verses.verse:
Though glad at home, and merry with guests,
A man shall be wary and wise.
The sage and shrewd, wide wisdom seeking,
Must see that his speech be fair.
A fool is he named who nought can say,
For such is the way of the witless
verses.means:
Be happy at home and merry with guests, but stay wise.
Speak well.
Someone who has nothing to say is called a fool.

verses.verse:
I found the old giant, now back have I fared,
Small gain from silence I got.
Full many a word, my will to get,
I spoke in Suttung's hall
verses.means:
The High One visited the old giant Suttung.
Silence won him nothing there, so he spoke many words to get his way.

verses.verse:
The mouth of Rati made room for my passage,
And space in the stone he gnawed.
Above and below the giants' paths lay,
So rashly I risked my head
verses.means:
The drill called Rati bored a path through the stone for him.
The High One risked his life to reach the mead.

verses.verse:
Gunnloth gave on a golden stool,
A drink of the marvelous mead.
A harsh reward did I let her have,
For her heroic heart,
And her spirit troubled sore
verses.means:
Gunnloth gave the High One a drink of the marvelous mead, upon a golden stool.
Winning it came at a cost, and the High One honors her brave heart.

verses.verse:
The well-earned beauty well I enjoyed,
Little the wise man lacks.
So Othrörir now has up been brought,
To the midst of the men of earth
verses.means:
He brought the mead of poetry, called Othrörir, out into the world of people.
That is where the gift of poetry comes from.

verses.verse:
Hardly, methinks, would I home have come,
And left the giants' land,
Had not Gunnloth helped me, the maiden good,
Whose arms about me had been
verses.means: The High One honors Gunnloth, the good maiden whose help brought him safely home from the land of the giants.

verses.verse:
The day that followed, the frost-giants came,
Some word of Hor to win,
And into the hall of Hor.
Of Bolverk they asked, were he back midst the gods,
Or had Suttung slain him there?
verses.means: The next day the frost giants came asking whether Bolverk, the High One in disguise, had returned or been slain.

verses.verse:
On his ring swore Othin the oath, methinks.
Who now his troth shall trust??
Suttung's betrayal he sought with drink,
And Gunnloth to grief he left
verses.means:
The High One swore by his ring, and outwitted the giant Suttung, to win the mead of poetry for gods and men.
Gunnloth was left in grief, and the stanza remembers the cost of that great gift.

verses.verse:
It is time to chant from the chanter's stool.
By the wells of Urth I was,
I saw and was silent, I saw and thought,
And heard the speech of Hor.
Of runes heard I words, nor were counsels wanting,
At the hall of Hor,
In the hall of Hor.
Such was the speech I heard
verses.means:
Now the High One speaks from the singer's seat.
By the well of Urth he watched in silence, and listened, and learned.

verses.verse:
I rede thee, Loddfafnir! and hear thou my rede,
Profit thou hast if thou hearest,
Great thy gain if thou learnest,
Rise not at night, save if news thou seekest,
Or fain to the outhouse wouldst fare
verses.means:
Here begin the lessons for Loddfafnir.
Listen, and you will gain.
Do not wander out at night unless you must.

verses.verse:
I rede thee, Loddfafnir! and hear thou my rede,
Profit thou hast if thou hearest,
Great thy gain if thou learnest,
Beware of sleep on a witch's bosom,
Nor let her limbs ensnare thee
verses.means:
Listen, Loddfafnir.
Do not let a harmful person lull you to sleep or tangle you up.

verses.verse:
Such is her might that thou hast no mind,
For the council or meeting of men.
Meat thou hatest, joy thou hast not,
And sadly to slumber thou farest
verses.means: Their power can make you lose your mind for your friends and your work, until you are sad and alone.

verses.verse:
I rede thee, Loddfafnir! and hear thou my rede,
Profit thou hast if thou hearest,
Great thy gain if thou learnest,
Seek never to win the wife of another,
Or long for her secret love
verses.means:
Listen, Loddfafnir.
Never try to take someone else's partner.

verses.verse:
I rede thee, Loddfafnir! and hear thou my rede,
Profit thou hast if thou hearest,
Great thy gain if thou learnest,
If o'er mountains or gulfs thou fain wouldst go,
Look well to thy food for the way
verses.means:
Listen, Loddfafnir.
Before you cross mountains or deep valleys, pack enough food for the way.

verses.verse:
I rede thee, Loddfafnir! and hear thou my rede,
Profit thou hast if thou hearest,
Great thy gain if thou learnest,
An evil man thou must not let,
Bring aught of ill to thee.
For an evil man will never make,
Reward for a worthy thought
verses.means:
Listen, Loddfafnir.
Do not let a bad person bring harm to you.
They will never repay a good thought.

verses.verse:
I saw a man who was wounded sore,
By an evil woman's word.
A lying tongue his death-blow launched,
And no word of truth there was
verses.means:
The High One saw a man brought down by cruel lies.
Words can wound deeply.

verses.verse:
I rede thee, Loddfafnir! and hear thou my rede,
Profit thou hast if thou hearest,
Great thy gain if thou learnest,
If a friend thou hast whom thou fully wilt trust,
Then fare to find him oft.
For brambles grow and waving grass,
On the rarely trodden road
verses.means:
Listen, Loddfafnir.
Visit the friends you trust often.
A path no one walks soon fills with brambles and grass.

verses.verse:
I rede thee, Loddfafnir! and hear thou my rede,
Profit thou hast if thou hearest,
Great thy gain if thou learnest,
A good man find to hold in friendship,
And give heed to his healing charms
verses.means:
Listen, Loddfafnir.
Find a good person to be your friend, and take their healing advice.

verses.verse:
I rede thee, Loddfafnir! and hear thou my rede,-,
Profit thou hast if thou hearest,
Great thy gain if thou learnest,
Be never the first to break with thy friend,
The bond that holds you both.
Care eats the heart if thou canst not speak,
To another all thy thought
verses.means:
Listen, Loddfafnir.
Never be the first to break a friendship.
It eats at the heart when you have no one to share your thoughts with.

verses.verse:
I rede thee, Loddfafnir! and hear thou my rede,
Profit thou hast if thou hearest,
Great thy gain if thou learnest,
Exchange of words with a witless ape,
Thou must not ever make
verses.means:
Listen, Loddfafnir.
Do not argue with someone who will not listen to reason.

verses.verse:
For never thou mayst from an evil man,
A good requital get.
But a good man oft the greatest love,
Through words of praise will win thee
verses.means:
You will never get a good reward from a bad person.
But a good person will often speak well of you and win you friends.

verses.verse:
Mingled is love when a man can speak,
To another all his thought.
Nought is so bad as false to be,
No friend speaks only fair
verses.means:
Real friends can tell each other everything they think.
Nothing is worse than being false, and a true friend tells you the truth, not only nice things.

verses.verse:
I rede thee, Loddfafnir! and hear thou my rede,
Profit thou hast if thou hearest,
Great thy gain if thou learnest,
With a worse man speak not three words in dispute,
Ill fares the better oft,
When the worse man wields a sword
verses.means:
Listen, Loddfafnir.
Do not quarrel with a worse person.
Even a good person can lose when the other has a sword.

verses.verse:
I rede thee, Loddfafnir! and hear thou my rede,-,
Profit thou hast if thou hearest,
Great thy gain if thou learnest,
A shoemaker be, or a maker of shafts,
For only thy single self.
If the shoe is ill made, or the shaft prove false,
Then evil of thee men think
verses.means:
Listen, Loddfafnir.
Make shoes or arrows only for yourself.
If they turn out badly, people will think badly of you.

verses.verse:
I rede thee, Loddfafnir! and hear thou my rede,
Profit thou hast if thou hearest,
Great thy gain if thou learnest,
If evil thou knowest, as evil proclaim it,
And make no friendship with foes
verses.means:
Listen, Loddfafnir.
Call wrong what it is, and do not make friends with those who mean harm.

verses.verse:
I rede thee, Loddfafnir! and hear thou my rede,
Profit thou hast if thou hearest,
Great thy gain if thou learnest,
In evil never joy shalt thou know,
But glad the good shall make thee
verses.means:
Listen, Loddfafnir.
You will find no joy in doing wrong.
Goodness will make you glad.

verses.verse:
I rede thee, Loddfafnir! and hear thou my rede,
Profit thou hast if thou hearest,
Great thy gain if thou learnest,
Look not up when the battle is on,
Like madmen the sons of men become,
Lest men bewitch thy wits
verses.means:
Listen, Loddfafnir.
In a battle, keep your head down and your mind clear.

verses.verse:
I rede thee, Loddfafnir! and hear thou my rede,-,
Profit thou hast if thou hearest,
Great thy gain if thou learnest,
If thou fain wouldst win a woman's love,
And gladness get from her,
Fair be thy promise and well fulfilled.
None loathes what good he gets
verses.means:
Listen, Loddfafnir.
If you hope to win someone's love, make fair promises, and keep them.

verses.verse:
I rede thee, Loddfafnir! and hear thou my rede,-,
Profit thou hast if thou hearest,
Great thy gain if thou learnest,
I bid thee be wary, but be not fearful.
Beware most with ale or another's wife,
And third beware lest a thief outwit thee
verses.means:
Listen, Loddfafnir.
Be careful, but do not be afraid.
Watch out most with ale, and for those who would trick you.

verses.verse:
I rede thee, Loddfafnir! and hear thou my rede,-,
Profit thou hast if thou hearest,
Great thy gain if thou learnest,
Scorn or mocking ne'er shalt thou make,
Of a guest or a journey-goer
verses.means:
Listen, Loddfafnir.
Never mock a guest or a traveler.

verses.verse:
Oft scarcely he knows who sits in the house,
What kind is the man who comes.
None so good is found that faults he has not,
Nor so wicked that nought he is worth
verses.means:
When someone new comes in, you can't tell right away what kind of person they are.
Nobody is so good that they have no faults, and nobody is so bad that they are worth nothing.

verses.verse:
I rede thee, Loddfafnir! and hear thou my rede,
Profit thou hast if thou hearest,
Great thy gain if thou learnest,
Scorn not ever the gray-haired singer,
Oft do the old speak good.
Oft from shrivelled skin come skillful counsels,
Though it hang with the hides,
And flap with the pelts,
And is blown with the bellies
verses.means:
Listen, Loddfafnir.
Never scorn an old storyteller.
The old often give the best advice.

verses.verse:
I rede thee, Loddfafnir! and hear thou my rede,
Profit thou hast if thou hearest,
Great thy gain if thou learnest,
Curse not thy guest, nor show him thy gate,
Deal well with a man in want
verses.means:
Listen, Loddfafnir.
Do not curse a guest or show them the door.
Be good to someone in need.

verses.verse:
Strong is the beam that raised must be,
To give an entrance to all.
Give it a ring, or grim will be,
The wish it would work on thee
verses.means:
The door that welcomes everyone must be strong.
Be generous, or your stinginess will come back to you.

verses.verse:
I rede thee, Loddfafnir! and hear thou my rede,
Profit thou hast if thou hearest,
Great thy gain if thou learnest,
When ale thou drinkest seek might of earth,
For earth cures drink, and fire cures ills,
The oak cures tightness, the ear cures magic,
Rye cures rupture, the moon cures rage,
Grass cures the scab, and runes the sword-cut.
The field absorbs the flood
verses.means:
Listen, Loddfafnir.
The earth, fire and the old remedies each help with something.
Nature has many ways to heal.

verses.verse:
Now are Hor's words spoken in the hall,
Kind for the kindred of men,
Cursed for the kindred of giants,
Hail to the speaker, and to him who learns!!
Profit be his who has them!!
Hail to them who hearken!
verses.means:
Now the High One's words have been spoken in the hall.
Hail to the one who speaks them, and to all who listen and learn.

verses.verse:
I ween that I hung on the windy tree,
Hung there for nights full nine.
With the spear I was wounded, and offered I was,
To Othin, myself to myself,
On the tree that none may ever know,
What root beneath it runs
verses.means: The High One tells how he hung on the windy tree for nine nights, wounded by the spear and offered, himself to himself, on the tree whose roots no one knows.

verses.verse:
None made me happy with loaf or horn,
And there below I looked.
I took up the runes, shrieking I took them,
And forthwith back I fell
verses.means:
No one brought him bread or drink.
He looked down, took up the runes, cried out, and fell back.

verses.verse:
Nine mighty songs I got from the son,
Of Bolthorn, Bestla's father.
And a drink I got of the goodly mead,
Poured out from Othrörir
verses.means: He learned nine mighty songs, and drank the precious mead of poetry.

verses.verse:
Then began I to thrive, and wisdom to get,
I grew and well I was.
Each word led me on to another word,
Each deed to another deed
verses.means:
Then he began to grow wise and strong.
Each word led to another word, and each deed to another deed.
Learning builds on itself.

verses.verse:
Runes shalt thou find, and fateful signs,
That the king of singers colored,
And the mighty gods have made.
Full strong the signs, full mighty the signs,
That the ruler of gods doth write
verses.means: There are runes to find, signs of great power, made by the gods and written by the ruler of the gods.

verses.verse:
Othin for the gods, Dain for the elves,
And Dvalin for the dwarfs,
Alsvith for giants and all mankind,
And some myself I wrote
verses.means: Each people had someone who carved their runes: Othin for the gods, Dain for the elves, Dvalin for the dwarfs.

verses.verse:
Knowest how one shall write, knowest how one shall rede??
Knowest how one shall tint, knowest how one makes trial??
Knowest how one shall ask, knowest how one shall offer??
Knowest how one shall send, knowest how one shall sacrifice?
verses.means:
Do you know how to write the runes, read them, and use them rightly?
Knowledge comes with care.

verses.verse:
Better no prayer than too big an offering,
By thy getting measure thy gift.
Better is none than too big a sacrifice,
So Thund of old wrote ere man's race began,
Where he rose on high when home he came
verses.means:
It is better to offer nothing than too much.
Give in measure with what you have received.

verses.verse:
The songs I know that king's wives know not,
Nor men that are sons of men.
The first is called help, and help it can bring thee,
In sorrow and pain and sickness
verses.means:
The High One knows songs that few know.
The first is called Help.
It brings comfort in sorrow, pain and sickness.

verses.verse:
A second I know, that men shall need,
Who leechcraft long to use
verses.means:
The second song is for those who heal.
The rest of this stanza is lost.

verses.verse:
A third I know, if great is my need,
Of fetters to hold my foe.
Blunt do I make mine enemy's blade,
Nor bites his sword or staff
verses.means: The third song blunts an enemy's blade, so it cannot harm.

verses.verse:
A fourth I know, if men shall fasten,
Bonds on my bended legs.
So great is the charm that forth I may go,
The fetters spring from my feet,
Broken the bonds from my hands
verses.means: The fourth song breaks bonds and fetters, so one can walk free.

verses.verse:
A fifth I know, if I see from afar,
An arrow fly 'gainst the folk.
It flies not so swift that I stop it not,
If ever my eyes behold it
verses.means: The fifth song stops an arrow flying toward the people.

verses.verse:
A sixth I know, if harm one seeks,
With a sapling's roots to send me.
The hero himself who wreaks his hate,
Shall taste the ill ere I
verses.means: The sixth song turns harm back on the one who sends it.

verses.verse:
A seventh I know, if I see in flames,
The hall o'er my comrades' heads.
It burns not so wide that I will not quench it,
I know that song to sing
verses.means: The seventh song puts out a fire raging over a hall full of friends.

verses.verse:
An eighth I know, that is to all,
Of greatest good to learn.
When hatred grows among heroes' sons,
I soon can set it right
verses.means:
The eighth song is the most useful of all.
When anger grows between people, it can set things right.

verses.verse:
A ninth I know, if need there comes,
To shelter my ship on the flood.
The wind I calm upon the waves,
And the sea I put to sleep
verses.means: The ninth song calms the wind and the waves, and puts the sea to sleep to keep a ship safe.

verses.verse:
A tenth I know, what time I see,
House-riders flying on high.
So can I work that wildly they go,
Showing their true shapes,
Hence to their own homes
verses.means: The tenth song sends night riders flying back to their own homes.

verses.verse:
An eleventh I know, if needs I must lead,
To the fight my long-loved friends.
I sing in the shields, and in strength they go,
Whole to the field of fight,
Whole from the field of fight,
And whole they come thence home
verses.means: The eleventh song keeps friends safe, so they go out whole and come home whole.

verses.verse:
A twelfth I know, if high on a tree,
I see a hanged man swing.
So do I write and color the runes,
That forth he fares,
And to me talks
verses.means:
The twelfth song lets the High One carve and color the runes,
so that one who has died may speak,
and share the wisdom of those who came before.

verses.verse:
A thirteenth I know, if a thane full young,
With water I sprinkle well.
He shall not fall, though he fares mid the host,
Nor sink beneath the swords
verses.means: The thirteenth song protects a young warrior, so they do not fall in battle.

verses.verse:
A fourteenth I know, if fain I would name,
To men the mighty gods.
All know I well of the gods and elves,
Few be the fools know this
verses.means:
The fourteenth song lets him name all the gods and elves.
Few know this.

verses.verse:
A fifteenth I know, that before the doors,
Of Delling sang Thjothrörir the dwarf.
Might he sang for the gods, and glory for elves,
And wisdom for Hroptatyr wise
verses.means: The fifteenth song was sung by the dwarf Thjothrörir, bringing strength to the gods, glory to the elves and wisdom to the High One.

verses.verse:
A sixteenth I know, if I seek delight,
To win from a maiden wise.
The mind I turn of the white-armed maid,
And thus change all her thoughts
verses.means: The sixteenth song can turn someone's heart toward love.

verses.verse:
A seventeenth I know, so that seldom shall go,
A maiden young from me
verses.means:
The seventeenth song is about keeping love close.
The rest of this stanza is lost.

verses.verse:
Long these songs thou shalt, Loddfafnir,
Seek in vain to sing.
Yet good it were if thou mightest get them,
Well, if thou wouldst them learn,
Help, if thou hadst them
verses.means:
Loddfafnir may long wish to sing these songs.
It would be good to have them, and helpful to learn them.

verses.verse:
An eighteenth I know, that ne'er will I tell,
To maiden or wife of man,
The best is what none but one's self doth know,
So comes the end of the songs,
Save only to her in whose arms I lie,
Or who else my sister is
verses.means:
The eighteenth song he will never tell anyone, except the one closest to his heart.
Some things are best kept to yourself.
